screens.title: Virtual Switching System (VSS) and StackWise Virtual (SVL)
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will explore how Cisco VSS and StackWise Virtual let two physical switches present a single control and management plane. You will learn the architectural principle that unifies two chassis, the role of the Virtual Switch Link or StackWise Virtual Link for synchronization, and how Multi-Chassis EtherChannel gives access devices true chassis-level redundancy. We’ll ground abstract ideas with a practical Starter Code sequence for two Catalyst 9500 switches and show how to verify that the virtual domain is healthy. This matters because it reduces Spanning Tree complexity at the access layer, improves bandwidth utilization, and gives near-instant failure recovery at the chassis level. You’ll also encounter common pitfalls to avoid, such as mismatched domain IDs, incorrect VSL configuration, and insufficient VSL bandwidth that can cause split-brain or a provisioned-only state. By the end of this chapter you should be able to explain the key components, run the basic configuration steps, and interpret the important show commands that confirm an operational SVL or VSS deployment. Consider how combining two switches into one logical unit changes your failure and maintenance planning.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Virtual Switching System
Virtual Switching System (VSS) and StackWise Virtual (SVL)
Chassis-level redundancy by making two switches behave as one logical device

This chapter explains how two switches share a single control plane and management interface through a dedicated high-bandwidth link. You will see why this reduces Spanning Tree complexity, increases bandwidth utilization with MEC, and provides fast failover when a member switch fails.

You will identify the roles inside a virtual switch pair and describe how Multi-Chassis EtherChannel enables true chassis-level redundancy. You will also run verification commands to confirm SVL health and interpret the output for Active and Standby roles. Finally, you will be able to diagnose common misconfigurations such as mismatched domain IDs or VSL settings and apply the correct troubleshooting steps. screens.title: What VSS and StackWise Virtual Are
screens.narratorSegment: Virtual Switching System and StackWise Virtual are technologies that let two independent switch chassis operate as a single logical switch. That single logical switch exposes one control plane and one management plane to the network. In practical terms this means routing protocols, Spanning Tree calculations, and management sessions run against one logical device instead of two separate ones. The principal benefit is chassis-level redundancy: if one chassis fails, the other continues forwarding and control functions with minimal interruption. A concrete example is a data center access pair where each server has two NICs; with MEC the server uses NICs terminated on different chassis but sees them as one aggregated link. A common misconception is to equate VSS/SVL with first-hop redundancy protocols like HSRP. HSRP protects only a routed gateway; VSS/SVL protects the entire switch chassis and all services running on it. Another potential confusion is the naming: VSS historically applies to Catalyst 6500/6800 platforms while StackWise Virtual is the Catalyst 9000 family equivalent, but both share the same architectural goal. Takeaway: VSS/SVL change failure and management models — plan maintenance, software versions, and VSL capacity with that single-logical-switch mindset.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: VSS and SVL unify two physical switches into a single logical switch, providing a shared control plane and chassis-level redundancy.

content.html:
Core Concept
What VSS / SVL mean

VSS and StackWise Virtual allow two switches to appear and behave as a single logical switch, sharing control plane and management while keeping independent dataplane hardware.

Why it matters
Simplifies topology, removes blocked STP links at access layer, and reduces operational complexity.
Concrete example
A server with two NICs can connect across both switches using MEC and keep a single logical link if one chassis fails.
Common misconception
This is not just first-hop redundancy; it is a full chassis unification, not equivalent to HSRP or VRRP.
Key Takeaway

Design and operate the pair as a single logical switch; that changes failure, upgrade, and verification practices.

Annotated architecture
Switch A
Control and dataplane hardware present locally
Switch B
Standby control plane synchronizes state with Active
The two members exchange control and synchronization over a dedicated VSL or SVL implemented as a high-bandwidth EtherChannel. If one member fails, the remaining member performs stateful switchover and continues to provide full switching and routing services.
Analogy
Think of two servers mirrored for process state where one runs and the other is ready to take over instantly.
Reflection
How would treating two switches as one change your maintenance window planning?

screens.title: VSS vs StackWise Virtual
screens.narratorSegment: VSS and StackWise Virtual share the same architectural goal: two physical switches act as a single logical switch with a unified control plane. The main distinction is platform and implementation history. VSS historically refers to Catalyst 6500 and 6800 series, while StackWise Virtual is the implementation for the Catalyst 9000 family, such as the 9300, 9400, and 9500 models. Functionally, both rely on a dedicated link—VSL or SVL—implemented as a high-bandwidth EtherChannel carrying control and synchronization traffic. A concrete example is a pair of Catalyst 9500s forming an SVL using two 10 gigabit links aggregated into a port-channel. A common misconception is that the technologies differ in behavior; in practice they provide the same logical unification, failover behavior, and MEC support, but commands and provisioning steps differ slightly by platform. When planning, it is important to consult platform-specific provisioning commands and IOS-XE support. The practical takeaway is to treat them as equivalent design patterns but follow the vendor-prescribed provisioning and verification commands for the platform in use. VSS vs StackWise Virtual means vss and svl are architecturally similar; the differences are primarily platform-specific commands and supported hardware.. In practical terms, platform differences, shared architecture, and naming clarity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Comparison
VSS (6500/6800)
Historically used on Catalyst 6500/6800 platforms. Uses VSL to synchronize control plane and state.
Often found in larger chassis-based campus cores.
Terminology and show commands are platform-specific.
Comparison
StackWise Virtual (Catalyst 9000)
The Catalyst 9000 family equivalent. Uses SVL as the dedicated link and supports the same logical unification and MEC capabilities.
Common in modern access and distribution designs for enterprise networks.
Provisioning commands like switch provision and switch virtual link differ by platform.
Practical note
When designing, focus on the logical behavior and required VSL capacity. Then follow the platform's provisioning steps and verify software compatibility. Treat both as the same design pattern but with platform-specific commands.

screens.title: VSL / SVL Link Design and Redundancy
screens.narratorSegment: The Virtual Switch Link or StackWise Virtual Link is the lifeline between the two members. It must carry control-plane messages, synchronization data, and often data-plane transit. For these reasons it is implemented as a dedicated high-bandwidth EtherChannel, commonly using multiple 10 gigabit ports or higher. A robust design uses at least two physical links bundled into a port-channel and, when possible, multiple member links for redundancy. If the VSL fails, a dangerous split-brain can occur where both switches assume the Active role. To mitigate this, enable dual-active detection methods—EtherChannel-based detection or BFD-based mechanisms where supported. Concrete example: build Port-channel100 from two 10G interfaces on each switch and mark it as the SVL. A common misconfiguration is reusing those interfaces for other services or not setting them to no switchport and channel-group consistently on both sides, which prevents the port-channel from forming. The takeaway is to treat the VSL as a critical system resource: dedicate capacity, validate physical health, and test dual-active detection to avoid unstable failovers. VSL / SVL Link Design and Redundancy means implement the vsl as a dedicated, high-bandwidth etherchannel with redundant member links and dual-active detection to avoid split-brain.. In practical terms, how to build a robust vsl using aggregated links and dual-active detection. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Implement the VSL as a dedicated, high-bandwidth EtherChannel with redundant member links and dual-active detection to avoid split-brain.

Process Flow
VSL planning steps
1
Choose dedicated ports
Select physical interfaces solely for the VSL; do not share them with other services.
2
Aggregate into port-channel
Bundle multiple links to form the VSL and provide higher bandwidth and redundancy.
3
Enable dual-active detection
Configure EtherChannel or BFD-based detection to prevent split-brain if the VSL fails.
4
Test and monitor
Validate port-channel formation and VSL health under failure scenarios before production use.
Concrete example
Use two 10G links per switch, aggregate them into Port-channel100, mark it as switch virtual link 1 and ensure interfaces are no switchport and channel-group mode on on both members.
Common mistake

Reusing VSL ports for other traffic or having mismatched channel-group modes prevents formation and may block the SVL formation.

screens.title: Active and Standby Roles and Stateful Switchover
screens.narratorSegment: Within a virtual switch pair, one member is elected Active and the other Standby. The Active member runs the control plane — routing protocols, STP, and management functions. The Standby member synchronizes configuration and state so that if the Active fails, the Standby can assume control quickly through Stateful Switchover. SSO preserves forwarding tables and other state so traffic continues flowing with minimal interruption. A concrete example is a routing adjacency: the Active maintains BGP or OSPF adjacency and the Standby synchronizes necessary state; after a failure, the Standby continues those functions without requiring full re-convergence from downstream devices. A common misunderstanding is expecting identical hardware behavior in the Standby; while the Standby mirrors much state, certain transient hardware counters or local-only processes may not be synchronized. The practical takeaway is to ensure your Standby has matching configuration and software level and that synchronization of critical state is validated during lab testing before production conversion. Also, verifying SSO timing and MEC behavior under failover helps set realistic RTO expectations. Active and Standby Roles and Stateful Switchover means active handles control plane, standby synchronizes state; stateful switchover enables rapid takeover with preserved network state.. In practical terms, how roles are assigned and how sso preserves forwarding state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Active handles control plane, Standby synchronizes state; Stateful Switchover enables rapid takeover with preserved network state.

content.html:
Definition
Active vs Standby
The Active member runs the control plane. The Standby keeps synchronized state and is ready to become Active through SSO if needed.
Stateful Switchover
SSO preserves forward and control state so takeover completes with minimal disruption.
Practical check
Verify that routing table, MAC table, and port-channel state are consistent across members during lab failover tests.
Example scenario
If Active fails, Standby performs SSO and takes over routing and switching functions. Downstream devices do not need to change their HSRP or routes because the logical switch identity remains the same.
Misconception
Standby is not a passive box; it must be kept synchronized and ready — mismatched configs prevent smooth SSO.
Takeaway
Treat both members as active parts of a single device for upgrades, monitoring, and capacity planning.

screens.title: Multi-Chassis EtherChannel (MEC)
screens.narratorSegment: Multi-Chassis EtherChannel allows one logical EtherChannel to terminate across both physical switches in a virtual pair. From the access device’s perspective, it’s a single aggregated link; behind the scenes, the physical member links are split across the two chassis. A concrete example is a server with two NICs: one NIC is connected to Switch A and the other to Switch B. Both links form a single EtherChannel and provide full aggregated bandwidth. If Switch A fails, the server maintains connectivity through the link to Switch B without requiring STP reconvergence or a MAC-table relearn in many cases, because MEC preserves the logical aggregation. A common misconception is that MEC removes all need for STP or redundancy design — MEC simplifies access-layer redundancy but the VSL and port-channel configurations must be correct and robust. Practical implications include simplified topology, better bandwidth utilization than blocked STP links, and reliance on correct port-channel hashing and load distribution strategies. The takeaway is that MEC directly enables chassis-level redundancy and should be used when the access device supports it. Multi-Chassis EtherChannel (MEC) means mec lets a downstream device form one logical etherchannel whose member links terminate on both physical switches, enabling seamless failover and full bandwidth utilization.. In practical terms, how mec gives access devices true chassis-level redundancy. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: MEC lets a downstream device form one logical EtherChannel whose member links terminate on both physical switches, enabling seamless failover and full bandwidth utilization.

content.html:
Core Concept
Multi-Chassis EtherChannel (MEC)
A single logical EtherChannel whose member links end on both switches of a virtual pair, giving the downstream device true chassis-level redundancy.
Concrete example
Server NIC 1 to Switch A and NIC 2 to Switch B form one EtherChannel from the server's perspective.
Why it matters
MEC eliminates blocked STP links and enables full use of aggregated bandwidth with chassis redundancy.
Operational notes
  • Ensure consistent port-channel and LACP modes across both physical switch terminations.
  • Confirm hashing and load distribution strategies to avoid imbalance across member links.
  • Test failover by bringing down one member link and observing continued connectivity.
Key Takeaway

Use MEC to provide seamless chassis-level redundancy for servers and access switches while fully utilizing aggregated bandwidth.

screens.title: Basic Configuration Steps for SVL/VSS
screens.narratorSegment: Configuring a basic StackWise Virtual or VSS domain follows a specific sequence. First, provision each physical switch with its switch number and model string as required for the platform. This registers the hardware identity used by the virtual domain. Second, select and configure the physical interfaces that will form the VSL and aggregate them into a port-channel. Ensure those interfaces are set to no switchport and channel-group mode on as appropriate. Third, create the port-channel interface and mark it as the virtual link with the switch virtual link command and a consistent link ID on both switches. Fourth, define the switch virtual domain with the same domain ID on each member so they recognize each other as peers. Finally, save, reload, and allow the switches to form the virtual stack; after conversion, manage configuration from the Active member. A common pitfall is ordering commands incorrectly or forgetting to make the VSL interfaces dedicated, which prevents the VSL from forming. Always test in a lab, confirm all prechecks, and schedule a maintenance window for conversion in production. Basic Configuration Steps for SVL/VSS means provision switch numbers, configure vsl port-channel, define the virtual domain id, save and reload — then verify formation from the active member.. In practical terms, provisioning switch numbers, domain id, and creating the vsl port-channel. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Common Misconfigurations and Troubleshooting Steps
screens.narratorSegment: There are a handful of recurring misconfigurations that prevent a successful VSS or StackWise Virtual formation. First, mismatched switch virtual domain IDs on the two members will stop them from recognizing each other — verify the domain ID is identical. Second, mismatched VSL or port-channel configuration, such as inconsistent channel-group IDs, differing channel modes, or leaving interfaces as switchport, will prevent the port-channel from forming and thus the VSL cannot be established. Third, incompatible provisioning commands or mismatched model strings and software versions can leave a switch in a PROVISIONED state. Physical issues like bad cables or wrong transceivers also occur. To troubleshoot, first confirm domain ID and provisioning strings, then check port-channel member state with show etherchannel summary, inspect interface status, and review logs. If the VSL fails and the pair could split, ensure dual-active detection is configured to prevent both members from becoming active. The takeaway is to validate configuration parity and physical health before reload and to use the verification commands systematically when diagnosing failures. Troubleshooting
Common problems
  • Mismatched domain ID: both switches must have identical switch virtual domain values.
  • VSL port-channel mismatch: inconsistent channel-group or interface config prevents formation.
  • Provisioning mismatch or software version: incompatible provision string or IOS-XE levels keep a switch provisioned only.
  • Physical link issues: cabling, SFPs, or transceiver mismatches can stop the VSL from coming up.
Resolution steps
  1. Confirm identical switch virtual domain on both members.
  2. Verify port-channel member status using show etherchannel summary.
  3. Check provisioning commands and IOS-XE versions for parity.
  4. Test physical interfaces and swap transceivers or cables if needed.
  5. Enable and verify dual-active detection to prevent split-brain in VSL failures.

screens.title: Operational Best Practices and Safety Notes
screens.narratorSegment: Operational best practices are critical when deploying VSS or StackWise Virtual. Always schedule conversions within a maintenance window and inform affected teams. Validate software versions and provisioning strings so both members are compatible before you convert. Treat the VSL as a high-importance link: dedicate capacity and ensure redundancy so a single fiber loss does not create a split-brain. Enable dual-active detection mechanisms supported by your platform — EtherChannel-based or BFD-based schemes — to detect a failed VSL and avoid both members becoming Active. Test failover scenarios in the lab to understand the real-world recovery time and behavior of MECs and SSO. Back up configurations before conversion and have rollback steps ready in case the virtual pair does not form. A typical misconception is that conversion is trivial; in production, the stakes are high because misconfiguration can cause widespread MAC-table corruption and instability. The core takeaway is to treat virtual switching as a major topology change: verify software, cabling, configuration parity, and dual-active detection before committing to production. Operational Guidance
Checklist before conversion
  • Confirm IOS-XE versions and provisioning strings match across both members.
  • Dedicate VSL interfaces and ensure redundant physical links in the port-channel.
  • Enable dual-active detection and validate behavior under failure scenarios.
  • Backup running-configuration and plan a rollback before reloading.
  • Schedule a maintenance window and run lab tests that simulate real traffic patterns.
Why this matters
A failed or misconfigured VSL can cause both switches to think they are Active, producing MAC flapping and network instability. Proper planning and detection reduce that risk.
Operational Tip

Document all configuration steps, and perform a dry-run in an isolated lab to validate rollback steps and expected timings for SSO.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: These three key concepts will guide design and operation of virtual switch deployments. First, the VSL or SVL is a dedicated, high-bandwidth EtherChannel that carries control-plane and synchronization traffic; it must be robust and redundant. Second, Multi-Chassis EtherChannel provides true chassis-level redundancy by letting downstream devices form a single EtherChannel across both chassis. Third, Active/Standby roles and Stateful Switchover enable rapid takeover with preserved forwarding state, but both members must be kept in sync and run compatible software. Keep these ideas at the forefront when planning, configuring, and verifying VSS or StackWise Virtual systems. They govern your maintenance windows, verification steps, and troubleshooting priorities. Ask yourself: have I dedicated sufficient VSL capacity, validated MEC behavior, and enabled dual-active detection before converting production switches? fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will explore how Cisco VSS and StackWise Virtual let two physical switches present a single control and management plane. You will learn the architectural principle that unifies two chassis, the role of the Virtual Switch Link or StackWise Virtual Link for synchronization, and how Multi-Chassis EtherChannel gives access devices true chassis-level redundancy. We’ll ground abstract ideas with a practical Starter Code sequence for two Catalyst 9500 switches and show how to verify that the virtual domain is healthy. This matters because it reduces Spanning Tree complexity at the access layer, improves bandwidth utilization, and gives near-instant failure recovery at the chassis level. You’ll also encounter common pitfalls to avoid, such as mismatched domain IDs, incorrect VSL configuration, and insufficient VSL bandwidth that can cause split-brain or a provisioned-only state. By the end of this chapter you should be able to explain the key components, run the basic configuration steps, and interpret the important show commands that confirm an operational SVL or VSS deployment. Consider how combining two switches into one logical unit changes your failure and maintenance planning.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain the architecture and benefits of Cisco Virtual Switching System and StackWise Virtual, and you will be able to configure a basic domain with SVL or VSL. You will identify the roles inside a virtual switch pair and describe how Multi-Chassis EtherChannel enables true chassis-level redundancy. You will also run verification commands to confirm SVL health and interpret the output for Active and Standby roles. Finally, you will be able to diagnose common misconfigurations such as mismatched domain IDs or VSL settings and apply the correct troubleshooting steps. Each objective builds a practical capability: understanding when to use virtual switching, preparing and provisioning switches, forming the VSL, verifying MECs, and preventing split-brain. A concrete example you will practice is provisioning two Catalyst 9500 switches, creating a port-channel as the SVL, assigning switch numbers and domain ID, and then using show commands to confirm both members are joined and roles are correct. Think of these objectives as a checklist for safely converting two standalone switches into a reliable virtual pair.

This second objectives slide focuses on hands-on skills and safety practices. You will provision switch numbers and models, create the SVL port-channel, set the switch virtual domain ID, and perform the reload sequence required to convert switches into the virtual pair. You will learn the sequence of checks to run after conversion, including verifying which member is Active and which is Standby, confirming the VSL is up, and ensuring MEC bundles are formed correctly on downstream devices. The practical example in this chapter is configuring two Catalyst 9500 switches using two 10 gigabit links as the SVL. You will practice interpreting output such as role indicators and port-channel summaries. You will also learn the precautions to take before conversion: schedule a maintenance window, validate IOS-XE compatibility, check cabling and port modes, and verify VSL bandwidth. This objective prepares you to convert real hardware safely and to anticipate and resolve the common issues that prevent a successful virtual switch formation.

Virtual Switching System and StackWise Virtual are technologies that let two independent switch chassis operate as a single logical switch. That single logical switch exposes one control plane and one management plane to the network. In practical terms this means routing protocols, Spanning Tree calculations, and management sessions run against one logical device instead of two separate ones. The principal benefit is chassis-level redundancy: if one chassis fails, the other continues forwarding and control functions with minimal interruption. A concrete example is a data center access pair where each server has two NICs; with MEC the server uses NICs terminated on different chassis but sees them as one aggregated link. A common misconception is to equate VSS/SVL with first-hop redundancy protocols like HSRP. HSRP protects only a routed gateway; VSS/SVL protects the entire switch chassis and all services running on it. Another potential confusion is the naming: VSS historically applies to Catalyst 6500/6800 platforms while StackWise Virtual is the Catalyst 9000 family equivalent, but both share the same architectural goal. Takeaway: VSS/SVL change failure and management models — plan maintenance, software versions, and VSL capacity with that single-logical-switch mindset.

VSS and StackWise Virtual share the same architectural goal: two physical switches act as a single logical switch with a unified control plane. The main distinction is platform and implementation history. Within a virtual switch pair, one member is elected Active and the other Standby. The Active member runs the control plane — routing protocols, STP, and management functions. The Standby member synchronizes configuration and state so that if the Active fails, the Standby can assume control quickly through Stateful Switchover. SSO preserves forwarding tables and other state so traffic continues flowing with minimal interruption. A concrete example is a routing adjacency: the Active maintains BGP or OSPF adjacency and the Standby synchronizes necessary state; after a failure, the Standby continues those functions without requiring full re-convergence from downstream devices. A common misunderstanding is expecting identical hardware behavior in the Standby; while the Standby mirrors much state, certain transient hardware counters or local-only processes may not be synchronized. The practical takeaway is to ensure your Standby has matching configuration and software level and that synchronization of critical state is validated during lab testing before production conversion. Also, verifying SSO timing and MEC behavior under failover helps set realistic RTO expectations. Multi-Chassis EtherChannel allows one logical EtherChannel to terminate across both physical switches in a virtual pair. From the access device’s perspective, it’s a single aggregated link; behind the scenes, the physical member links are split across the two chassis. A concrete example is a server with two NICs: one NIC is connected to Switch A and the other to Switch B. Both links form a single EtherChannel and provide full aggregated bandwidth. If Switch A fails, the server maintains connectivity through the link to Switch B without requiring STP reconvergence or a MAC-table relearn in many cases, because MEC preserves the logical aggregation. A common misconception is that MEC removes all need for STP or redundancy design — MEC simplifies access-layer redundancy but the VSL and port-channel configurations must be correct and robust. Practical implications include simplified topology, better bandwidth utilization than blocked STP links, and reliance on correct port-channel hashing and load distribution strategies. The takeaway is that MEC directly enables chassis-level redundancy and should be used when the access device supports it. There are a handful of recurring misconfigurations that prevent a successful VSS or StackWise Virtual formation. First, mismatched switch virtual domain IDs on the two members will stop them from recognizing each other — verify the domain ID is identical. Second, mismatched VSL or port-channel configuration, such as inconsistent channel-group IDs, differing channel modes, or leaving interfaces as switchport, will prevent the port-channel from forming and thus the VSL cannot be established. Third, incompatible provisioning commands or mismatched model strings and software versions can leave a switch in a PROVISIONED state. Physical issues like bad cables or wrong transceivers also occur. To troubleshoot, first confirm domain ID and provisioning strings, then check port-channel member state with show etherchannel summary, inspect interface status, and review logs. If the VSL fails and the pair could split, ensure dual-active detection is configured to prevent both members from becoming active. The takeaway is to validate configuration parity and physical health before reload and to use the verification commands systematically when diagnosing failures. Validate software versions and provisioning strings so both members are compatible before you convert. These three key concepts will guide design and operation of virtual switch deployments. First, the VSL or SVL is a dedicated, high-bandwidth EtherChannel that carries control-plane and synchronization traffic; it must be robust and redundant. Second, Multi-Chassis EtherChannel provides true chassis-level redundancy by letting downstream devices form a single EtherChannel across both chassis. Third, Active/Standby roles and Stateful Switchover enable rapid takeover with preserved forwarding state, but both members must be kept in sync and run compatible software. Keep these ideas at the forefront when planning, configuring, and verifying VSS or StackWise Virtual systems. They govern your maintenance windows, verification steps, and troubleshooting priorities.
